newsitem.title: USA: Republican scores surprise win in New Mexico vote.
newsitem.headline: Republican scores surprise win in New Mexico vote.

text.p: The Republican Party scored a major upset on Tuesday by winning a special election for the New Mexico congressional seat left vacant by U.N. ambassador Bill Richardson.

Republican candidate Bill Redmond claimed victory after election officials said he scored 42 per cent support with virtually all the results in from the Third Congressional District of northern New Mexico, while his Democratic rival Eric Serna trailed with 40 percent.

Green Party candidate Carol Miller, who drew support away from Serna, had 17 percent. Albuquerque television station KOAT said its own final tally from all the polling stations showed exactly the same results.
Richardson, a Democrat, had comfortably held the House of Representatives seat for 14 years before taking his present post of ambassador to the United Nations in February.

Registered Democrats outnumber Republicans more than two-to-one in the district but Serna's campaign was hurt by questions over his political past, a low turnout and the defection of some Democrats to the Green Party.
Redmond, a 43-year-old Christian minister, ran an aggressive campaign, accusing Serna of misusing public money and political influence as a member of New Mexico's State Corporation Commission.

"I feel great because I believe northern New Mexico is at the beginning of a new chapter in our history," Redmond said in a victory speech to supporters on Tuesday night. "We have a message that is basically family and new jobs."
Serna had characterized Redmond as a right-wing extremist intent on imposing an anti-abortion and anti-gun control agenda, but appealed for cross-party cooperation as his rival claimed victory.
"Let's work together, let's respect one another, let's go forward with a vision of inclusiveness," a smiling Serna told reporters.
With Redmond's victory, Republicans now hold a 228-to-206 lead over Democrats in the House, with one independent who usually votes with the Democrats.
In last year's election, Richardson beat Redmond with 67 percent of the vote but the Republican Party had predicted it could win this time around.
"It is an amazing upset," said Chris Garcia, a political scientist at the University of New Mexico.
Other analysts said Serna's campaign was weakened by internal divisions over the Democratic Party's candidate selection process, and that many registered Democrats stayed away from the polls.
